ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT At least five people died and 87 were missing after the passenger ferry caught fire near Coron, in Palawan province, on Wednesday evening. The Philippine Coast Guard said 42 people had been rescued. The ferry was travelling from Manila with 134 people aboard, including 117 passengers and 17 crew members. The vessel sent a distress signal about four nautical miles from Turda village. Strong currents later carried it further offshore. Rough weather and high waves have hampered the search. Authorities have not determined the cause of the fire. Coast guard teams are continuing rescue operations, and the number of people missing or rescued may change. Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPA US news At Trump meeting, Xi Jinping lays out terms to avoid US-China military conflict Chinese president’s proposals for lessening tensions come amid period of intense competition between the two countries over AI and trade Trump-Xi summit – latest updates Robert Tait in Washington Thu 24 Sep 2026 11.52 EDT Last modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 13.53 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Xi Jinping has called for extensive cooperation with Washington to avoid the “Thucydides trap” that could put the US and China on a military collision course amid rising tensions over artificial intelligence, trade and Taiwan. At the start of his summit meeting with Donald Trump in the White House, the Chinese president laid out terms for a mutual understanding that he said could steer the two competing superpowers away from future military conflict and on to a road of mutual gain. Rather than confrontation, conditions for “achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again go hand in hand” should be the goal Xi said, citing Trump’s political catchphrase. “We should strengthen communication. China and the United States are different in national conditions, but through candid, in-depth and continued dialog, our two countries can understand each other better, seek common ground while shelving differences, and build up mutual trust,” said Xi, with Trump looking on. “We should coexist in peace,” he said. “China and the United States, as two major countries, stand to gain from cooperation and will both lose in confrontation. Our two militaries should maintain regular dialog and improve mechanisms for crisis communication and prevention.” With such conditions in place, Xi said, “the Thucydides trap can be overcome”, refering to the phenomenon, defined by the Greek historian, of tensions that arise when an emerging power challenges the dominance of an established power. Xi invoked the phrase in his meeting with Trump in Beijing in May, asking the US president how he planned to avoid it. His proposals for lessening tensions – which also included the invitation of 100,000 young Americans to visit China on student exchanges – come amid a period of intense competition between the two powers over artificial intelligence and trade, with each side imposing tariffs on the other. Trump had earlier welcomed Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, to the White House, noting that he was the first Chinese leader to make a second state visit to the US. The previous visit occurred in 2015, when Barack Obama was US president. “President Xi and Madame Peng arrive at an important moment for America, the 250th anniversary of our founding,” he said. Trump said that he had forged “a truly great friendship” with Xi. “President Xi and I have made tremendous strides on the issues facing our two countries,” he said. “Our teams have been working to encourage a more balances trading relationship, including the new market access for American farmers and ranchers.” He said the current visit would include discussion overs security, technology and AI – which he called “super intelligence”, a term he introduced in his speech to the United Nations general assembly on Tuesday. Xi also extolled his personal relationship with his American counterpart, saying: “President Trump and I have respect for each other. We have built personal rapport and stayed in touch.” Addressing Trump directly, he said: “During your visit to China this year, we agreed to build a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability. I am ready to work with you to steer the giant ship of the China-US relationship on a steady course towards the future.” The White House welcome ceremony came after Trump had taken the unusual step of going to Andrews air force base in Maryland the evening before to greet the Chinese leader and his wife on the tarmac. Much of the same pageantry was repeated in Thursday’s ceremony, with both countries’ national anthems being played. Trump was flanked by his wife, Melania, while members of his cabinet and senior aides – including Natalie Harp, Trump’s dedicated assistant nicknamed “the human printer” by fellow staffers – looked on. Trump and Xi were scheduled to hold bilateral talks after the ceremony and the welcoming speeches. Despite the harmonious tone adopted by both leaders, analysts have voiced scepticism about the possibility of longstanding stable arrangements being arrived at over a host of issues. In the race for AI, the US has placed strict export controls on microchips, semiconductors, software and chipmaking equipment in a bid to slow China’s development. A truce agreed between Trump and Xi in South Korea last year aimed at keeping tariffs lower had been due to expire in November but has now been extended until February, the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent said. Analysts believe the extension suggests Trump continues to be dissatisfied with Xi’s concession offers on trade and wants to keep the pressure on in the hope of getting a better deal if the two meet again at the G20 summit scheduled to be held in Miami in December. Despite the trade war between the two countries, Chinese imports have continue to surge into the US. China is on course to run a $1tn trade deficit for the second year running. Bos , Worthy News Europe Bureau Chief reporting from Budapest, Hungary BUDAPEST, HUNGARY ( Worthy News ) – Hungary’s new government is moving to dismantle key restrictions affecting homosexual and transgender people introduced under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, including rules that effectively prevented gay people from adopting children. Prime Minister Péter Magyar confirmed that his cabinet will change the Orbán-era adoption system, under which unmarried applicants require approval from the minister responsible for family affairs. The restriction, introduced in 2020, effectively halted adoption by same-sex couples because Hungary does not allow them to marry. Before the change, gay or lesbian couples could effectively adopt when one partner applied as a single person. New here? Receive the Worthy Brief and stay informed from a biblical perspective. Hungary’s constitution defines marriage as a voluntary union between “one man and one woman.” It also states that family relationships are based on marriage and the parent-child relationship and declares: “The mother is a woman, the father is a man.” Same-sex couples can enter registered partnerships in Hungary, but these do not provide the same adoption rights as marriage. ADOPTION RULES CHANGING “We can state unequivocally that we will change this system,” Magyar said. Magyar, a self-declared right-wing conservative, appeared to open the door to adoptions by gay couples, saying individual decisions should be made by child-protection professionals rather than politicians. However, speaking to Hungary’s Kossuth Radio, he stopped short of explicitly promising full joint-adoption equality for same-sex couples. Yet Magyar signaled a significant change in tone toward Hungary’s homosexual community, saying people should be free to love whom they choose and should not face hostility because of their sexual orientation. “Love is free, it is a fundamental right, and in a humane country this cannot be a question,” Magyar added. ‘LOVE IS FREE’ He said homosexual as well as heterosexual Hungarians, believers, atheists, Budapest residents and people living in the countryside should have a voice in discussions surrounding a planned new constitution. The shift comes amid a wider crisis in Hungary’s child-protection system, with a government investigation documenting physical and sexual abuse, neglect, hunger, staff shortages and inadequate placements for vulnerable children. Magyar has questioned whether a traumatized child without a family is necessarily better off in institutional care than with a loving same-sex couple. His cabinet is also rewriting controversial 2021 “child protection” legislation introduced under Orbán that restricted content related to LGBTQ+ issues accessible to minors. Under legislation submitted to parliament Monday, references to promoting or portraying homosexuality, gender transition or departure from birth-sex identity would be removed from those restrictions. LGBTQ+ REFERENCES REMOVED Instead, the proposed law focuses on pornography, age-inappropriate sexual material and content promoting sexual violence, exploitation, grooming or other sexual crimes, as well as material considered seriously harmful to a child’s development. The move follows an April ruling by the European Union’s top court that Hungary violated EU law through restrictions on content related to LGBTQ+ issues that the court concluded discriminated against and stigmatized gay and transgender people. Magyar explained that changing the legislation could help Hungary avoid financial penalties linked to the dispute and assist efforts to recover about 500 million euros ($590 million) in European Union education funding. Orbán had defended the so-called child protection law as part of what he viewed as Hungary’s defense of traditional Christian family values, despite criticism from LGBTQ+ activists and the European Union. His government later expanded the legislation to effectively ban Pride gatherings, allowing authorities to prohibit rallies deemed to violate the child-protection measures and introducing fines for participants. PRIDE GATHERINGS TARGETED The measures prompted mass demonstrations in Budapest and criticism from European officials and human rights groups, who argued that child protection was being used to restrict freedom of assembly and the rights of sexual minorities. Orbán rejected such criticism, portraying his policies as protecting children and Hungary’s traditional understanding of family against what he viewed as increasingly liberal Western attitudes toward sexuality and gender. Magyar’s approach marks a significant departure from those policies, although his government says it seeks to strengthen protections for children after revelations about severe failures in Hungary’s state-care system. During Orbán’s rule, Hungary also ended legal recognition of gender changes in official documents and imposed restrictions on educational and media content concerning LGBTQ+ issues. Yet Magyar has left open how far the changes concerning same-sex couples will extend. Lift this up in Prayer 12 people are currently praying.
